title: Vector product
summary: The [[vector-product|vector product]] $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ turns two vectors into a new vector at right angles to both. Its length is the area of the parallelogram they make, so half of it gives a triangle's area. It is the zero vector exactly when the two vectors are parallel.

goals.text: Work out $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ from components, and use the [[right-hand-screw-rule|right-hand screw rule]] to say which way it points.
Find a vector, or a unit vector, perpendicular to two given vectors.

Expand and simplify vector products with their rules, including $\boldsymbol{w} \times \boldsymbol{v} = -\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ and $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$.
Use $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} = \boldsymbol{0}$ to show that non-zero vectors are parallel, or to find an unknown that makes them parallel.
Find the area of a parallelogram or a triangle from $\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert$, exactly or to 3 s.f.

synonyms: area of a triangle with vectors

before.hint: Square each component, add, then take the square root.

before.prompt: P is $(3, -1, 2)$ and Q is $(1, 2, 5)$. Find $\overrightarrow{PQ}$.
before.hint: Start at P and end at Q, so subtract the coordinates of P from those of Q.
Perpendicular vectors have a scalar product of $0$.
before.explain: $1 \times 2 + 2 \times 0 + (-2) \times 1 = 0$, so the scalar product is $0$. The others give $8$ and $-3$. Revise it in {{lesson:3.13}}.

blocks.text: In {{lesson:3.13}} the [[scalar-product|scalar product]] turned two vectors into a number. The [[vector-product|vector product]] turns two vectors into a new vector. That vector is perpendicular to both of the ones you started with.

Why would you want that? Draw $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ from the same point. If they are not parallel, together they fix one flat plane. A vector at right angles to that plane is what you need for planes in {{lesson:3.17}}, and its length measures area.
There are two directions at right angles to the plane: one side of it and the other. A rule called the [[right-hand-screw-rule|right-hand screw rule]] picks one of them.

blocks.statement: The vector product of $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ is the vector $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} = \lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta\,\boldsymbol{n}$. The angle $\theta$ from $\boldsymbol{v}$ to $\boldsymbol{w}$ lies from $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$. The vector $\boldsymbol{n}$ has length $1$, is perpendicular to both $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$, and points the way the right-hand screw rule gives.
blocks.plain: It is read v cross w, and it is also called the cross product.

blocks.text: Read the definition in two parts. The number $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta$ is the length. The [[unit-vector|unit vector]] $\boldsymbol{n}$ only gives the direction.

The right-hand screw rule: point the fingers of your right hand along $\boldsymbol{v}$. Curl them towards $\boldsymbol{w}$ through the angle $\theta$. Your thumb now points along $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$.
The name comes from an ordinary screw. Turn it from $\boldsymbol{v}$ towards $\boldsymbol{w}$ and it moves in the direction of $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$.

blocks.alt: Vectors v and w are drawn from the same point in a flat shaded plane, with the angle theta between them and a curved arrow turning from v towards w. The vector v cross w points straight up out of the plane. A dashed vector w cross v points straight down, the opposite way.
blocks.caption: Turning from $\boldsymbol{v}$ to $\boldsymbol{w}$ gives $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ upwards. Turning the other way gives $\boldsymbol{w} \times \boldsymbol{v}$ downwards.

blocks.text: For example, take the [[base-vectors|base vectors]] $\boldsymbol{i}$ and $\boldsymbol{j}$. They are perpendicular unit vectors, so the length of $\boldsymbol{i} \times \boldsymbol{j}$ is $1 \times 1 \times \sin 90^{\circ} = 1$. Curl your fingers from the $x$-axis to the $y$-axis and your thumb points up the $z$-axis, so $\boldsymbol{i} \times \boldsymbol{j} = \boldsymbol{k}$.
In practice you don't use the angle. You work out the vector product from components with this formula. It is in the formula booklet, so you don't need to memorise it.
A way to read it: for the first component, cover the first row of both vectors and cross-multiply what is left, $v_{2}w_{3} - v_{3}w_{2}$. Do the same for the third component, covering the third row.
The middle component is the odd one. Covering the second row gives $v_{1}w_{3} - v_{3}w_{1}$, and you must change its sign. That is why the booklet writes it as $v_{3}w_{1} - v_{1}w_{3}$.

blocks.question: Find $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ for $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{w} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}$.
steps: Check it is perpendicular to both with scalar products: $2(-10) + (-1)(7) + 3(9) = 0$ and $1(-10) + 4(7) + (-2)(9) = 0$. Both are $0$, so the answer passes.

blocks.text: Getting the middle component with the wrong sign. It is $v_{3}w_{1} - v_{1}w_{3}$, the other way round from the pattern of the first and third. The scalar product check catches this slip.

blocks.hint: Write the vectors as columns. The second vector has no $\boldsymbol{j}$ term, so its middle component is $0$.
blocks.explain: Use $\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$. The components are $3(1) - (-2)(0) = 3$, then $(-2)(4) - 1(1) = -9$, then $1(0) - 3(4) = -12$.

blocks.text: Because $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ is perpendicular to both vectors, dividing it by its length gives a unit vector perpendicular to both. Its negative works too: it points the other way along the same line.

blocks.question: Find a unit vector perpendicular to both $\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}$.
steps: Any multiple of the vector product is perpendicular to both, so start there: $\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}(0)(-1) - (-1)(2)\\(-1)(0) - (3)(-1)\\(3)(2) - (0)(0)\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\6\end{pmatrix}$.
Divide by the length to make a unit vector. The vector $-\frac{1}{7}\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\6\end{pmatrix}$ is an equally good answer.

blocks.text: The length of $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ has its own booklet formula. Use it when you know two lengths and the angle between them, but not the components.

blocks.tex: \lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert = \lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta, \text{ where } \theta \text{ is the angle between } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w}

blocks.prompt: $\lvert\boldsymbol{a}\rvert = 5$, $\lvert\boldsymbol{b}\rvert = 4$ and the angle between $\boldsymbol{a}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}$ is $150^{\circ}$. Find $\lvert \boldsymbol{a} \times \boldsymbol{b} \rvert$.

blocks.text: Finding an angle with $\sin\theta = \frac{\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert}{\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert}$. Both $\theta$ and $180^{\circ} - \theta$ have the same sine, and $\sin^{-1}$ only gives the acute one. Use the scalar product from {{lesson:3.13}} for angles.
[[vector-product|Vector products]] expand like brackets, just as scalar products do. There is one big difference: the order matters.

1. Swapping the order reverses the direction: $\boldsymbol{w} \times \boldsymbol{v} = -\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$. Curl your fingers from $\boldsymbol{w}$ to $\boldsymbol{v}$ and your thumb points the other way.
2. You can expand brackets: $\boldsymbol{u} \times (\boldsymbol{v} + \boldsymbol{w}) = \boldsymbol{u} \times \boldsymbol{v} + \boldsymbol{u} \times \boldsymbol{w}$.
3. A scalar moves to the front: $(k\boldsymbol{v}) \times \boldsymbol{w} = k(\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w})$.
4. A vector crossed with itself gives the [[zero-vector|zero vector]]: $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$. The angle is $0^{\circ}$ and $\sin 0^{\circ} = 0$.

blocks.why: Swap $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ in the component formula. The first component $v_{2}w_{3} - v_{3}w_{2}$ becomes $w_{2}v_{3} - w_{3}v_{2}$, which is its negative, and the same happens to the other two.

blocks.text: Rules 2 and 3 can be checked the same way, one component at a time. Each component is ordinary arithmetic with numbers.
Treating $\boldsymbol{b} \times \boldsymbol{a}$ as $\boldsymbol{a} \times \boldsymbol{b}$ when you collect terms. Replace it with $-\boldsymbol{a} \times \boldsymbol{b}$ before you add.

blocks.question: Simplify $(\boldsymbol{a} + 2\boldsymbol{b}) \times (\boldsymbol{a} - \boldsymbol{b})$, giving your answer in terms of $\boldsymbol{a} \times \boldsymbol{b}$.
steps: Expand like two brackets, using rules 2 and 3, and keep every product in its order: $\boldsymbol{a} \times \boldsymbol{a} - \boldsymbol{a} \times \boldsymbol{b} + 2\boldsymbol{b} \times \boldsymbol{a} - 2\boldsymbol{b} \times \boldsymbol{b}$.

blocks.hint: Expand all four products in order. Then use $\boldsymbol{a} \times \boldsymbol{a} = \boldsymbol{0}$ and $\boldsymbol{b} \times \boldsymbol{a} = -\boldsymbol{a} \times \boldsymbol{b}$.

blocks.text: The rules also let you use a vector product you already know, without any components for the vectors themselves.

blocks.question: Given that $\boldsymbol{p} \times \boldsymbol{q} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\4\end{pmatrix}$, find $(2\boldsymbol{q}) \times (\boldsymbol{p} + \boldsymbol{q})$.
steps: Rule 3 moves the $2$ to the front: $2(\boldsymbol{q} \times \boldsymbol{p}) + 2(\boldsymbol{q} \times \boldsymbol{q})$.

blocks.text: If $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ are parallel, the angle between them is $0^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$. Both have $\sin\theta = 0$, so $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ has length $0$. It is the [[zero-vector|zero vector]].
The reverse is also true, as long as neither vector is the zero vector itself.

blocks.statement: For non-zero vectors, $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} = \boldsymbol{0}$ exactly when $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ are parallel.
blocks.why: $\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert = \lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta$ with $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert$ and $\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert$ not zero. So it is $0$ only when $\sin\theta = 0$, which means $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$.

blocks.text: Put this beside {{lesson:3.13}}. A zero [[scalar-product|scalar product]] means perpendicular. A zero [[vector-product|vector product]] means [[parallel-vectors|parallel]].

blocks.question: Use the vector product to show that $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}5\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{w} = \begin{pmatrix}-10\\2\\-6\end{pmatrix}$ are parallel.
steps: Both vectors are non-zero and their vector product is the zero vector, so they are parallel. Indeed $\boldsymbol{w} = -2\boldsymbol{v}$, so they point opposite ways.

blocks.question: The vectors $\begin{pmatrix}p\\2\\-3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\q\end{pmatrix}$ are parallel. Use the vector product to find $p$ and $q$.
steps: Parallel vectors have a vector product of $\boldsymbol{0}$: $\begin{pmatrix}p\\2\\-3\end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\q\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2q - 3\\-12 - pq\\-p - 8\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$.
Check the middle component: $-12 - (-8)\left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right) = -12 + 12 = 0$. All three are zero.

blocks.hint: Write out the second or third component in terms of $k$ and set it equal to $0$.
blocks.explain: The third component is $6k - (4)(3) = 6k - 12$, so $k = 2$. Then the first vector is $\tfrac{2}{3}$ of the second.

blocks.text: Three points A, B and C are [[collinear|collinear]] when $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ are parallel. They share the point A, so they lie on one line. That gives a quick test: $\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = \boldsymbol{0}$.

blocks.hint: Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$, then their vector product.
blocks.explain: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\6\\6\end{pmatrix}$, so $\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC} = \boldsymbol{0}$. A non-zero scalar product says nothing about being parallel.

blocks.text: Draw a parallelogram with adjacent sides $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ and the angle $\theta$ between them. Take $\boldsymbol{v}$ as the base.

blocks.alt: A parallelogram with base v along the bottom and side w leaving the same corner at angle theta. A dashed vertical height drops from the top of w to the base, meeting it at a right angle, and is labelled length of w times sine theta. A dashed diagonal joins the ends of v and w, cutting the parallelogram into two equal triangles, and the lower triangle is shaded.
blocks.caption: The height is $\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta$. The diagonal cuts the parallelogram into two equal triangles.

blocks.text: Area of a parallelogram is base times height. This is in the prior-learning section of the formula booklet. The base is $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert$ and the height is $\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta$, so the area is $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta$.
That is exactly $\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert$. So the length of the [[vector-product|vector product]] is the area of the parallelogram. This is in the booklet too.

blocks.tex: A = \lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert, \text{ where } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w} \text{ form two adjacent sides of a parallelogram}

blocks.text: A diagonal cuts the parallelogram into two equal triangles. So a triangle with sides $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ from the same corner has half the area. This matches $\frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ from {{lesson:3.2}}.

blocks.tex: A = \frac{1}{2}\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert, \text{ where } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w} \text{ form two sides of a triangle from the same vertex}

blocks.text: For triangle ABC, use two sides that leave the same corner, such as $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$. Don't use the position vectors of the points: they are arrows from the origin, not sides.

blocks.question: A parallelogram has adjacent sides $2\boldsymbol{i} + \boldsymbol{j} - \boldsymbol{k}$ and $\boldsymbol{i} - \boldsymbol{j} + 3\boldsymbol{k}$. Find its exact area.
steps: Write the sides as columns: $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{w} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$.

blocks.text: Forgetting the $\frac{1}{2}$ for a triangle, or halving for a parallelogram. $\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert$ is the parallelogram. The triangle is half of it.

blocks.question: The points $\mathrm{P}(1, -2, 3)$, $\mathrm{Q}(4, 0, 1)$ and $\mathrm{R}(-1, 3, 2)$ form a triangle. Use your calculator to find the area of triangle PQR. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
steps: Two sides from corner P: $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{PR} = \begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\\-1\end{pmatrix}$.
Write down what you put into the calculator: area $= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{8^{2} + 7^{2} + 19^{2}} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{474}$. This line earns the method mark.
The calculator gives $10.8857\ldots$. Round only now.

blocks.prompt: Find the area of the triangle with vertices $\mathrm{O}(0, 0, 0)$, $\mathrm{A}(3, 0, 4)$ and $\mathrm{B}(0, 2, 1)$. Give your answer to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: From the origin, the sides are just the position vectors of A and B. Find their vector product, then halve its length.

blocks.text: Exam questions often run this backwards: you are given the area and must find an unknown.

blocks.question: The triangle OAB has $\overrightarrow{OA} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\k\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Its area is $3$. Find the possible values of $k$.
steps: Set the triangle's area equal to $3$: $\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{5k^{2} + 1} = 3$, so $\sqrt{5k^{2} + 1} = 6$.
Square both sides: $5k^{2} + 1 = 36$, so $k^{2} = 7$. Both signs work, because squaring hides the sign of $k$.

blocks.prompt: $\mathrm{A}(0, 1, 1)$, $\mathrm{B}(2, 1, 0)$ and $\mathrm{D}(1, 3, 1)$ are three vertices of the parallelogram ABCD, where D is next to A. Find the area of ABCD.
blocks.hint: The adjacent sides from A are $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AD}$.
blocks.explain: $\overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AD} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\4\end{pmatrix}$, with length $\sqrt{4 + 1 + 16} = \sqrt{21}$. Halving gives the triangle ABD, not the parallelogram.

blocks.text: $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ is perpendicular to both $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$. Its direction follows the right-hand screw rule. Check your answer with two scalar products of $0$.
Order matters: $\boldsymbol{w} \times \boldsymbol{v} = -\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$. Brackets expand, scalars move to the front, and $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{0}$.

blocks.tex: \lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert = \lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta, \text{ where } \theta \text{ is the angle between } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w}

blocks.text: For non-zero vectors, $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} = \boldsymbol{0}$ means parallel, and $\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \boldsymbol{w} = 0$ means perpendicular.

blocks.tex: A = \lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert, \text{ where } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w} \text{ form two adjacent sides of a parallelogram}
A = \frac{1}{2}\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert, \text{ where } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w} \text{ form two sides of a triangle from the same vertex}

mistakes: Getting the middle component of the vector product wrong. It is $v_{3}w_{1} - v_{1}w_{3}$, so check that your answer has a scalar product of $0$ with both vectors.

Working out $\boldsymbol{w} \times \boldsymbol{v}$ when the question asks for $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$. The result points the opposite way, which matters for a direction or a later angle.

Using $\frac{\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert}{\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert}$ and $\sin^{-1}$ to find an angle. That only gives the acute angle, so use the scalar product, whose sign shows whether the angle is obtuse.

Crossing the position vector of a point with a side. Position vectors start at the origin, so use two displacement vectors that leave the same corner, such as $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$.
Missing out the $\frac{1}{2}$ for a triangle, or putting it in for a parallelogram. The length $\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert$ is the parallelogram's area.
Writing $\boldsymbol{b} \times \boldsymbol{a} = \boldsymbol{a} \times \boldsymbol{b}$ when expanding. Swapping the order changes the sign.
examTips: “Find” a vector perpendicular to two vectors: show each component of the vector product. A sign slip with no working gets no method mark, so write the products out.
“Use a vector method” for an area means showing the vector product and its length. Area from $\frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ alone may not earn the marks.
“Show that” vectors are parallel: work out all three components of the vector product, show each is $0$, and say the vectors are non-zero and so parallel.
On Paper 1, leave an area as an exact surd such as $\sqrt{62}$. On Paper 2, write the expression you put into the calculator and give the area to 3 s.f.
